text: I’ll model the barrel on the duct axis, with its base at \(z=0\). The stated fin stack is 102 mm tall, so I’ll center it on the 120 mm barrel, leaving 9 mm clear at each end. Because the dome profile is unspecified, I’ll assume a hemispherical 45 mm-radius head above \(z=120\) mm. The duct then spans \(z=-150\) to \(+420\) mm. I’ll first create the solid obstruction and surrounding fluid volume at metre scale, then inspect its topology and dimensions before exporting or meshing.

The first bounds check exposed a placement convention issue: `Box` is centred by default, so the duct was shifted by half its width and height. I’ll correct it using an explicit centre translation, rebuild the Boolean, and render a coarse preview of both the engine obstruction and the transparent duct.

The preview also reveals that `Cylinder` is centred axially in this installed build123d version: the barrel extended 60 mm below its intended base, and each fin was centred on its nominal lower face. I’ll correct both translations, remeasure the complete stack, and inspect the resulting fluid faces by analytic surface type so the patches can be assigned from the generating geometry rather than from bounding-box position.

The corrected preview now shows the intended 12-fin stack entirely on the 120 mm barrel. The fluid boundary consists of six duct planes, 24 annular fin faces plus 12 fin rims, exposed barrel segments (including its base), and one spherical head face. I’ll query the analytic face properties and the patch exporter interface, then form explicit face groups based on those generating surface types and radii.

I’ll now export all six requested patch classes in one coordinated tessellation. The fin group is identified by the 70 mm analytic cylindrical rims and their annular planar faces; the barrel uses the 45 mm cylindrical surfaces plus its exposed base disk; the head is the spherical face. The unchanged duct source faces are mapped directly into the cut fluid solid, with inlet and outlet defined on the two source planes at the specified axial stations. This avoids independently tessellated patch seams.

For meshing, I’ll use a 10 mm Cartesian duct background (30 × 30 × 57 cells) and let `snappyHexMesh` refine the engine surfaces two levels to 2.5 mm. That gives at least two cells across each 6 mm fin gap while keeping the first mesh moderate in size. The block itself carries the inlet, outlet, and four duct-wall faces; only the internal barrel, fin, and head STLs need to drive snapping, avoiding duplicate surfaces coincident with the block boundary.

The background mesh is correctly 0.30 × 0.30 × 0.57 m with 51,300 cells. I’ll now refine a compact box around the engine to level 2 and snap the three internal solid patch surfaces. No boundary layers are requested or assumed.

`snappyHexMesh` stopped before changing the block because this OpenFOAM release requires the standard numerical-scheme dictionaries even for mesh motion. I’ll add the minimal mesh-motion schemes and solver, then rerun the same meshing stage.

The installed distribution does not provide the usual shared `meshQualityDict` include at that path. I’ll locate its packaged quality template and reference the available file rather than inventing limits.
The packaged file is `meshQualityDict.cfg`; I’ll correct that single include and rerun.

The snapped mesh completed with 234,184 cells and retained all three engine patch names. I’ll run the binding `checkMesh` now and inspect the boundary table and cell-quality summary before rendering a longitudinal cut through the fin gaps.

The binding check found four highly skew faces (maximum 7.34), so this version is not acceptable. These occur on the finely curved internal boundary where the 2.5 mm cells are marginal for the 3 mm fin thickness. I’ll regenerate from the background and increase only the engine-surface refinement to level 3 (1.25 mm), leaving the surrounding refinement box at level 2.
The original block has been restored; I’ll run the level-3 surface snap and inspect its final quality report.
The targeted refinement produced 610,902 cells, with 1.25 mm cells adjacent to the engine and 2.5 mm cells through the surrounding fin region. I’ll rerun the binding mesh check.

The refined mesh passes `checkMesh`: one region, six patches, maximum non-orthogonality 56.0°, maximum skewness 2.69, and positive cell volumes. I’ll make a longitudinal \(y=0\) cut showing cell edges to verify that the narrow passages between all fin pairs are actually connected and resolved.

The longitudinal cut confirms open, meshed passages between every neighbouring fin pair and appropriate refinement around the dome, barrel, and fin rims. The geometry and mesh are complete; no requested geometric property remains unchecked.

The advisory report confirms complete one-to-one patch coverage but still labels that confirmation as a warning, so I will waive it as intentional. The meshing-point classifier disagrees with the CAD solid; before waiving it, I’ll explicitly test the point against the fluid Boolean and engine obstruction.

The CAD kernel confirms the meshing point is inside the duct fluid and outside the engine: its radius is 169.7 mm versus the engine’s 70 mm maximum. I’ll therefore waive the location classifier as a false advisory for this multiply bounded fluid surface, and waive the coverage notice because it itself reports every triangle assigned exactly once.
